newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers seek access to TWA wreckage.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers seek access to TWA wreckage.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, U.S. Law Correspondent

Lawyers representing the families of victims killed in last summer's crash of TWA Flight 800 urged a federal judge on Monday to order the National Transportation and Safety Board to give them access to the plane's wreckage.

Lee Kreindler, a New York lawyer who chairs the plaintiffs committee, told U.S. District Judge Robert Sweet that the lawyers and their investigators want an opportunity to view and photograph the wreckage stored at a hangar in Calverton, New York.

Sweet moved the hearing into chambers, from which he barred reporters. Following the closed session he did not make a ruling but said in open court that photographs had been made available to the public through the press.
He told lawyers, "We'll see if some kind of programme can be worked out."

The tragedy occurred on July 17 when the Paris-bound Boeing 747 exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean, just minutes after taking off from Kennedy International Airport. All 230 passengers and crew on board were killed.
About 70 lawsuits brought by the families of those victims have been consolidated in Manhattan federal court before Sweet.
Although the NTSB has not determined the cause of the explosion, the lawsuits allege the plane was destroyed by a mechanical malfunction that could have been prevented.
While the NTSB has allowed the families to view the plane, it has refused access to the lawyers and their investigators as part of the litigation information gathering process.

"It is not right to deny that same opportunity to the lawyers for these people, in this case," Kreindler argued in court papers. "The families look to us for information on the case. They want, and are entitled to our insight into what they have seen."
He alleged that the board had abused its discretion in denying the lawyers access.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Katherine Staton argued that the NTSB has complete discretion over access to the wreckage and that its decision is not reviewable.
Kreindler disagreed and said it was appropriate to challenge the decision in federal court.
Kreindler told reporters after the hearing that the NTSB plans to hold a public hearing in October or November and that it would probably not allow the lawyers access until after that time.
He and Michel Baumeister, another plaintiffs lawyer, also argued that the press had been allowed to view and photograph the wreckage.
"All we ask is that the families who have paid the highest price be put on the same equal footing," Baumeister told the judge.

CBS and CNN reported last weekend that investigators looking into reports of "missile" sightings before the TWA explosion now believe the streak of light that witnesses reported may actually have been a stream of burning fuel.

They said investigators believed an explosion in the jet's centre fuel tank spewed a trail of burning fuel that could explain witness reports of a mysterious streak of light, accounts that led to early theories the plane was brought down by a missile.
